topics.summary: A class wants to know its most popular game. What is data, and how do we find the answer from it?

content.text:
If you ask your classmates about their favourite colours, you will get a list of colours. This list is an example of data. Similarly, if you measure the weight of each student in your class, you would get a collection of measures of weight, again data.
Any collection of facts, numbers, measures, observations or other descriptions of things that convey information about those things is called data.
Navya and Naresh are discussing their favourite games.
Cricket is my favourite game!
I play cricket sometimes but hockey is the game I like the most.
I think cricket is the most popular game in our class.
I am not sure. How can we find the most popular game in our class?

1. Two friends disagree: one says cricket is the most popular game in the class, the other says hockey. Neither has asked anyone else.
2. Make a guess before the next step: how could the two friends find out for sure, and what would they have to write down?

content.text:
1. Predict first: Navya says cricket is the favourite of the class, because it is her favourite. Is one child's choice enough?
2. To find what the whole class likes, ask each student the same question: what is your favourite game?
3. Write each answer down. The list of answers collected is data.
4. Only the list of the whole class can tell the most popular game, not one child's opinion.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the list has 31 names with a game beside each. Can you read the most popular game straight off the list?

4. The group with the highest count is Hockey, so hockey is the most popular game, not cricket.

media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 4 'Data Handling and Presentation' (Collecting and Organising Data). Tally the sweet choices in fives. Find each total. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Tally Table Maker. Tally the sweet choices in fives. Find each total. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: Tallying turns a stream of answers into bundles of five, and the total of each row is its frequency.
tool_config.title: Tally Table Maker
tool_config.screen: A row of sweet names; answers appear one at a time as speech bubbles; a Tally button under each row adds a stroke, and the fifth stroke crosses the four; a total box and a most-chosen marker.
feedback: A fifth stroke tapped beside the four, not across, snaps into a bundle of five with a short note.
A wrong total lights up the bundles one by one with a count in fives.
A solved card shows the frequency table with the tally and the total side by side.
challenges: Tally 12 answers over 3 sweets and give each total (for example 5, 4 and 3).
Read a row of one bundle and 3 strokes (8).
Read a row of two bundles and 2 strokes (12).
Which sweet has the greatest frequency in a 20-answer stream? (the highest total)
Totals of all rows must equal the number of answers: 6 + 9 + 13 + 3 + 7 (38).
Which sweet has the least frequency, and by how much is it below the most? (3 and 10 fewer than 13)

Count the crossed bundles in fives, then the loose strokes.
Add 5 for each bundle and 1 for each loose stroke.

1. Predict first: five children call out their sweet one by one. How can you keep count without losing your place?
2. Make one stroke for each child. When the count reaches 5, draw the fifth stroke across the previous four to make a bundle of five.
3. To read a row, count the bundles in fives and then the loose strokes: one bundle and 1 stroke is 6 children.
4. Counting in bundles makes a long row quick and safe to read.

content.text: Teacher's Note: Provide more opportunities to collect and organise data. Ask students to guess what is the most popular colour, game, toy, school subject, etc., amongst the students in their classroom and then collect the data for it. It can be a fun activity in which they also learn about their classmates. Discuss how they can organise the data in different ways, each way having its own advantages and limitations. content.text:
1. Predict first: the ordered list has 27 numbers. Is there a shorter way to show the same data?
2. Count each size: size 3 occurs 3 times, size 4 occurs 9 times, size 5 occurs 10 times, size 6 occurs 4 times and size 7 occurs 1 time.
3. The frequency table is short, and the ordered list shows every single entry. Each way has its own advantages.
4. To find how many students wear a size larger than 4, add the frequencies of 5, 6 and 7.

media.description: A question from the book asks you to count five letters in a newspaper item and put them in order of frequency. The video gives the plan of tallying, reading, comparing and ordering, and says why most classmates get the same order.

video_script.why: The child runs the whole plan of collecting, counting and ordering on their own data and explains why classmates agree.

marks.ask: a question mark lights up above the letters
marks.scene: the title card arrives with the sheet and the news item
marks.letters: the five letters light up one after another

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a news item from a newspaper.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>You count five letters in its words: see, ee, eye, ar and ex.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which of these five letters will you meet the most?
beats.on_screen: title card with a small newspaper item pasted on a sheet, and the five letters c, e, i, r and x written beside it Photo: A folded newspaper on a table

marks.think: Kiko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.
beats.on_screen: the news item, the five letters and the question mark stay on the board

marks.many: the letters of the news item light up in many places
marks.plan: the empty table with its tally rows appears beside the item

narration: <bookmark mark='many'/>A news item holds many letters, so we need a plan for counting.
<bookmark mark='plan'/>We tally the letters one by one, and then read the counts.
beats.on_screen: the news item with many letters, and an empty table with one tally row for each of the five letters

marks.given: the given line is written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a small news item, and a table with a row for each of the five letters.
beats.on_screen: Given: a small news item, and a table with the letters c, e, i, r, x and one more letter of your choice

marks.find: the three lines to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the most, the least, and the order of the five letters.
beats.on_screen: To find: the letter found the most, the letter found the least, and the five letters in ascending order of frequency

marks.read: a pointer moves along the words and a tally mark is added in the table each time one of the five letters is met

narration: <bookmark mark='read'/>Step one, read the news item word by word, so no letter is missed.
Each time you meet one of the five letters, draw a tally mark in its row.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: read the news item word by word and draw a tally mark in the right row for each letter

marks.count: each row is read as bundles of five and loose strokes, and its count is written in the last row of the table

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step two, read each row of tally marks and write its count.
Count every bundle as five, because a bundle holds five, and then add the loose strokes.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: read each row of tally marks and write its count in the table

narration: <bookmark mark='most'/>Step three, compare the counts in the table, because they show which letter is found most.
The largest count belongs to the letter found the most.
<bookmark mark='least'/>The smallest count belongs to the letter found the least.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: compare the counts: the largest count is the letter found the most, the smallest count is the letter found the least

marks.order: the five letters slide into a row from the smallest count to the largest
marks.compare: the row is placed beside the rows of classmates

narration: <bookmark mark='order'/>Step four, list the five letters from the smallest count to the largest.
This is ascending order, so we can compare it with our classmates.
<bookmark mark='compare'/>Then compare your row with the rows of your classmates.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: write the five letters from the smallest count to the largest, then compare your row with your classmates

marks.again: the same plan is applied to a new news item
marks.friends: two friends show their own ways of counting beside yours

narration: <bookmark mark='friends'/>Step five, ask your friends how they counted, because we can learn their ways.
<bookmark mark='again'/>For another news item, the same plan works again.
beats.on_screen: Step 5: ask friends how they counted; the same plan works for another news item

marks.ans: the answer row of five letters is boxed
marks.why: the same row of letters appears over several news items
marks.ends: the last letter of the row is circled for the most and the first letter for the least

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Almost everyone gets the order ex, see, ar, eye, ee.
<bookmark mark='ends'/>The letter ee is found the most, and ex is found the least.
<bookmark mark='why'/>English words use the letters in much the same proportions in any news item.
beats.on_screen: Answer: almost everyone gets the order x, c, r, i, e; e is found the most and x the least

content.text:
Pictographs are one visual and suggestive way to represent data without writing any numbers. Look at this picture, you may be familiar with it from previous classes.
This picture helps you understand at a glance the different modes of travel used by students. Based on this picture, answer the following questions:
Which mode of travel is used by the most number of students?
Which mode of travel is used by the least number of students?
A pictograph represents data through pictures of objects. It helps answer questions about data with just a quick glance.

content.text:
Nand Kishor collected responses from the children of his middle school in Berasia regarding how often they slept at least $9$ hours during the night. He prepared a pictograph (key: triangle $= 10$ children): Always $5$ triangles; Sometimes $2$ triangles and a half triangle; Never $4$ triangles. Answer using the pictograph: $1$. What is the number of children who always slept at least $9$ hours at night? $2$. How many children sometimes slept at least $9$ hours at night? $3$. How many children always slept less than $9$ hours each night? Explain how you got your answer. $(1)$: Children who always slept at least $9$ hours $(2)$: Children who sometimes slept at least $9$ hours $(3)$: Children who always slept less than $9$ hours (Never)

content.text:
$1$. $5$ pictures: $5 \times 10 = 50$
$2$. $2$ full symbols $= 20$, half symbol $= 5$, so $20 + 5 = 25$
$3$. $4$ pictures for 'Never' means $40$ children never sleep $9$ hours, i.e. always sleep less than $9$ hours
Answer: $1$: $50$ children; $2$: $25$ children; $3$: $40$ children

Header row: first cell text 'Day'; second cell text 'Number of Books Borrowed' and, at the right end of that cell, one open-book symbol followed by the text '= 1 Book'. Below it, 6 data rows from top to bottom: row 1 label 'Monday' with 5 books; row 2 label 'Tuesday' with 4 books; row 3 label 'Wednesday' with 2 books; row 4 label 'Thursday' with no symbols (empty cell); row 5 label 'Friday' with 5 books; row 6 label 'Saturday' with 8 books. Open-book symbol: two equal rectangles side by side sharing one vertical spine line, fill BG, INK outline 2.5 px, three short horizontal INK lines inside each page; every book has the same size. No numbers are written beside any row. The Thursday row stays empty (no symbol, no zero written). Nothing is highlighted. All text is INK, sans-serif, at least 34 px high on a 1920 px canvas.

media.title: Pictograph Builder
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 4 'Data Handling and Presentation' (Pictographs). Pick a key. Drop symbols in the rows. Check. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Pictograph Builder. Pick a key. Drop symbols in the rows. Check. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A key is chosen so that each frequency becomes a few symbols, and a half symbol shows half of the key.

tool_config.screen: A table of categories and numbers; a key picker for 1, 2, 5, 10 and 100; empty rows into which symbols and half symbols are dropped; a check strip that multiplies the symbols by the key.
feedback: A key that leaves a remainder other than half a key shows the leftover and asks for a better key.
Too many symbols in a row show a crowded warning that suggests a bigger key.
A solved card shows symbols times the key beside the table number.
challenges: Draw dogs 18, 36, 12, 48, 18, 24 with the key 6 (3, 6, 2, 8, 3, 4 symbols).

Why is the key 10 a poor choice for 33 students? (3 students cannot be shown)

Draw 7 books with the key 2 (3 symbols and a half).

content.text:
Sangita decided to use one smiley to represent 10 students instead.
Since she used one smiley to show 10 students, she had a problem in showing 25 students and 35 students in the pictograph. Then, she realised she could use a half smiley to show 5 students.
What could be the problems faced in preparing such a pictograph, if the total number of students present in a class is 33 or 27? (Math Talk)
It can be more challenging to prepare a pictograph when the amount of data is large or when the frequencies are not exact multiples of the scale or key.

content.text: Magan Bhai sells kites at Jamnagar. Six shopkeepers from nearby villages come to purchase kites from him. The number of kites he sold to these six shopkeepers are given below: Table: Chaman $250$, Rani $300$, Rukhsana $100$, Jasmeet $450$, Jetha Lal $250$, Poonam Ben $700$ kites. Prepare a pictograph using the symbol (kite) to represent $100$ kites. Answer: $(a)$: How many symbols represent the kites that Rani purchased? $(b)$: Who purchased the maximum number of kites? $(c)$: Who purchased more kites, Jasmeet or Chaman? $(d)$: Rukhsana says Poonam Ben purchased more than double the number of kites that Rani purchased. Is she correct? Why? $(a)$: Symbols for Rani $(b)$: Maximum kites $(c)$: Jasmeet or Chaman $(d)$: Is Rukhsana correct?

media.title: Bar Graph Reader
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 4 'Data Handling and Presentation' (Bar Graphs). Read the scale. Tap a bar. Turn its units into a value. Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Bar Graph Reader. Read the scale. Tap a bar. Turn its units into a value. Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

topics.summary: In a bar graph the length of each bar, read with the scale, gives the frequency; the longest bar is the most and the shortest bar is the least.

content.text:
Have you seen graphs like this on TV or in a newspaper?
Like pictographs, such bar graphs can help us to quickly understand and interpret information, such as the highest value, the comparison of values of different categories, etc. However, when the amount of data is large, presenting it by a pictograph is not only time consuming but at times difficult too. Let us see how data can be presented instead using a bar graph.
Let's take the data collected by Lakhanpal earlier, regarding the number of students absent on one day in each class:
He presented the same data using a bar graph:
Answer the following questions using the bar graph: 1. In Class 2, __ students were absent that day. 2. In which class were the maximum number of students absent? __ 3. Which class had full attendance that day? __
When making bar graphs, bars of uniform width can be drawn horizontally or vertically with equal spacing between them; then the length or height of each bar represents the given number. As we saw in pictographs, we can use a scale or key when the frequencies are larger.

content.text:
Let us look at an example of vehicular traffic at a busy road crossing in Delhi, which was studied by the traffic police on a particular day. The number of vehicles passing through the crossing each hour from 6 a.m. to 12:00 noon is shown in the bar graph. One unit of length stands for 100 vehicles.
We can see that the maximum traffic at the crossing is shown by the longest bar, i.e., for the time interval 7, 8 a.m. The bar graph shows that 1200 vehicles passed through the crossing at that time. The second longest bar is for 8, 9 a.m. During that time, 1000 vehicles passed through the crossing. Similarly, the minimum traffic is shown by the smallest bar, i.e., the bar for the time interval 6, 7 a.m. During that time, only about 150 vehicles passed through the crossing. The second smallest bar is that for the time interval 11 a.m., 12 noon, when about 600 vehicles passed through the crossing.
The total number of cars passing through the crossing during the two-hour interval 8.00, 10.00 a.m. as shown by the bar graph is about 1000 + 800 = 1800 vehicles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the population bars rise from 1951 to 2001. By how much did the population grow, and in which decade did it grow most?
2. Read each bar with the scale: 36, 44, 54, 68, 84 and 102 crores.
3. The growth over fifty years is 102 − 36 = 66 crores.
4. The growth in each decade is the difference of two neighbouring bars: 8, 10, 14, 16 and 18 crores, so the last decade grew most.

diagram_spec.manim_description: Draw a horizontal bar graph on a plain BG canvas, 16:9. Draw a vertical axis line at the left and a horizontal axis line at the bottom, both INK, 3 px, meeting at the bottom-left corner, no arrowheads. Along the vertical axis make six equal slots; label them from the bottom to the top in INK, right-aligned against the axis, each at the centre height of its bar: 6–7, 7–8, 8–9, 9–10, 10–11, 11–12. Write the axis title 'Time intervals' in INK, rotated 90 degrees to read upward, to the left of these labels. The horizontal axis is a value scale that starts at 0 on the vertical axis (no tick and no label for 0). Draw twelve equally spaced short tick marks in INK at 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 1100 and 1200, and write each number in INK, horizontal, under its tick. Extend the horizontal axis line to 1250 on the scale. Write the axis title 'Number of vehicles' in INK, centred below the tick numbers. Draw one horizontal bar in each slot, standing on the vertical axis, all of equal thickness (60 percent of the slot) with equal gaps, filled MARK_FILL with a 3 px INK outline. Bar lengths on the scale, from the bottom bar to the top bar: 6–7 = 150 (its end sits exactly midway between the ticks 100 and 200), 7–8 = 1200, 8–9 = 1000, 9–10 = 800, 10–11 = 700, 11–12 = 600. Draw no value labels on the bars, no gridlines, no chart title and no key.

the six values add up to 150 + 1200 + 1000 + 800 + 700 + 600 = 4450, the total the solution states, but the total is NOT drawn
no value labels, no total, no scale sentence in the image (the question diagram shows only what the question gives)
diagram_spec.alt_text: A horizontal bar graph of vehicles per hour: bars of 150, 1200, 1000, 800, 700 and 600 vehicles for 6–7, 7–8, 8–9, 9–10, 10–11 and 11–12, on a scale of 100 to 1200.
diagram_spec.render_note: The book's bar ends are read by eye (page picture, pdf p.14): 6–7 ends midway between the 100 and 200 ticks (150); 9–10 is drawn at about 820 but the book text and the LP use 800, so draw 800; 10–11 is drawn at about 695 and the LP says about 700, so draw 700; 7–8 (1200), 8–9 (1000) and 11–12 (600) end on their ticks. The drawn values are the LP / book-text values, not pixel readings. The book prints the tick numbers rotated; horizontal is used here for legibility.
diagram_spec.reason: The question is read off the Delhi traffic bar graph (six horizontal bars, 1 unit of length = 100 vehicles): the six bar lengths are the data and reading them against the scale is the skill. The book question has no numbers of its own; the values written in brackets in the LP text are the 'about' values read from these bars. Question figure = the graph as printed: no value labels, no total.

media.description: The bars of the traffic graph at a Delhi crossing are read with the scale of one hundred vehicles for one unit, and the six hourly counts are added. The sum is checked by adding the units first and multiplying by one hundred.

<bookmark mark='half'/>A bar of one and a half units stands for one hundred and fifty vehicles.

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, add the six readings in pairs, because small sums are safer to keep right.
<bookmark mark='sum1'/>One hundred and fifty and one thousand two hundred make one thousand three hundred and fifty.
<bookmark mark='second'/>One thousand and eight hundred make one thousand eight hundred.
<bookmark mark='third'/>Seven hundred and six hundred make one thousand three hundred.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, add the three pair sums, because that gives the total.
One thousand three hundred and fifty and one thousand eight hundred make three thousand one hundred and fifty.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three thousand one hundred and fifty and one thousand three hundred make four thousand four hundred and fifty.
That is the total.

narration: <bookmark mark='units'/>Step three, check by adding the units first, so that we are sure of the total.
The bars are one and a half, twelve, ten, eight, seven and six units.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>They add up to forty four and a half units.
<bookmark mark='times'/>Forty four and a half times one hundred gives four thousand four hundred and fifty.
It matches.

content.text:
A bar graph shows the population of India in each decade over $50$ years, in crores: $1951$: $36$, $1961$: $44$, $1971$: $54$, $1981$: $68$, $1991$: $84$, $2001$: $102$. The scale is $1\text{ unit}$ length for $10$ crores, so a bar of $5\text{ units}$ shows $50$ crores and a bar of $8\text{ units}$ shows $80$ crores. How much did the population of India increase over $50$ years? How much did it increase in each decade?
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S18.T18.C69.IMG1}}

topics.summary: To draw a bar graph, choose a scale, divide each frequency by it to get the bar height in units, and draw bars of equal width with equal gaps from zero.

content.text:
In a previous example, Shri Nilesh prepared a frequency table representing the sweet preferences of the students in his class. Let's try to prepare a bar graph to present his data, 
1. First, we draw a horizontal line and a vertical line. On the horizontal line, we will write the name of each of the sweets, equally spaced, from which the bars will rise in accordance with their frequencies; and on the vertical line we will write the frequencies representing the number of students.
2. We must choose a scale. That means we must decide how many students will be represented by a unit length of a bar so that it fits nicely on our paper. Here, we will take 1 unit length to represent 1 student.
3. For jalebi, we therefore need to draw a bar having a height of 6 units (which is the frequency of the sweet jalebi), and similarly for the other sweets we have to draw bars as high as their frequencies.
4. We, therefore, get a bar graph as shown below,

content.text:
When the frequencies are larger and we cannot use the scale of 1 unit length = 1 number (frequency), we need to choose a different scale like we did in the case of pictographs.
Example: The number of runs scored by Smriti in each of the 8 matches are given in the table below:
In this example, the minimum score is 0 and the maximum score is 100. Using a scale of 1 unit length = 1 run would mean that we have to go all the way from 0 to 100 runs in steps of 1. This would be unnecessarily tedious. Instead, let us use a scale where 1 unit length = 10 runs. We mark this scale on the vertical line and draw the bars according to the scores in each match. We get the following bar graph representing the above data.

diagram_spec.manim_description: Draw a vertical bar graph on a plain BG canvas, 16:9. Draw a vertical axis line at the left, rising to 3600 on the scale, and a horizontal baseline at the bottom, both INK, 3 px, meeting at the bottom-left corner, no arrowheads. On the vertical axis draw eighteen equally spaced short tick marks in INK, the first one full spacing above the baseline (the baseline is zero and has no tick and no label), and write the numbers in INK to the left of the ticks from bottom to top: 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, 1600, 1800, 2000, 2200, 2400, 2600, 2800, 3000, 3200, 3400, 3600. Each tick spacing is one unit length = ₹ 200. Write the axis title 'Expenditure (in ₹)' in INK, rotated 90 degrees to read upward, to the left of the numbers. Along the baseline make six equal slots, left to right, and write under each in INK, rotated 90 degrees to read upward: House rent, Food, Education, Electricity, Transport, Miscellaneous. Write the axis title 'Item' in INK, centred below the rotated labels. Draw one vertical bar in each slot, standing on the baseline, all of equal width (50 percent of the slot) with equal gaps, filled MARK_FILL with a 3 px INK outline. Bar tops sit exactly on tick positions, left to right: House rent = 3000 (15th tick), Food = 3400 (17th tick, the tallest bar), Education = 800 (4th tick), Electricity = 400 (2nd tick), Transport = 600 (3rd tick), Miscellaneous = 1200 (6th tick). Draw no value labels on the bars, no gridlines, no chart title and no key.

media.description: The bars for electricity and education in a family's spending graph are compared to see whether one is half of the other. Halving the larger amount and fitting two short bars into the tall bar both give the same answer, and Keeko's doubt, that half means the same height, is checked.

<bookmark mark='ask'/>Is the cost of electricity about half the cost of education?

narration: <bookmark mark='ten'/>Take a bar that is six units tall.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Split it into two equal parts, and each part is three units tall.
<bookmark mark='word'/>Each of the two equal parts is called half of the bar.
beats.on_screen: a bar of 10 squares split into two bars of 5 squares; the words two equal parts, half appear

narration: <bookmark mark='edu'/>Given, education costs eight hundred rupees, which is a bar of four units.
<bookmark mark='elec'/>Electricity costs four hundred rupees, which is a bar of two units.

marks.find: the question is written

beats.on_screen: To find: is the cost of electricity about half the cost of education?

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, split the cost of education into two equal parts, because that is half.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Eight hundred divided by two is four hundred.
beats.on_screen: Step 1: half of 800 is 800 / 2 = 400

marks.two: 400 and 400 are written side by side
marks.same: an equals sign appears between them

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, compare, because equal numbers show half.
Half of education is four hundred, and electricity costs four hundred.
<bookmark mark='same'/>The two numbers are the same.
beats.on_screen: Step 2: half of education is 400 and electricity is 400; the two numbers are the same

marks.copy: the electricity bar of 2 units is copied beside itself
marks.stack: the two copies are stacked and reach the top of the education bar

narration: <bookmark mark='copy'/>Step three, check on the graph, because a picture can confirm the numbers.

<bookmark mark='stack'/>They reach the top of the education bar, with no gap and no extra.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Two units and two units make four units.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: check on the graph. The 2-unit electricity bar is copied and stacked twice; 2 + 2 = 4 units, the height of the education bar

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Yes, the cost of electricity is exactly half the cost of education.
beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes, 400 is exactly half of 800

half of 800 = 800 / 2 = 400, which is the cost of electricity
check: 400 + 400 = 800, and 2 + 2 = 4 units
so electricity is exactly half of education

final_answer.value: Yes, 400 is exactly half of 800

content.text:

What is the scale for this graph? $(d)$: Draw the correct bar for Sagar. $(e)$: Add the scale of the bar graph by placing the correct numbers on the vertical axis. $(f)$: Are the bars for Seoni and Indore correct in this graph? If not, draw the correct bars.

content.text:
{{DIAGRAM:M3.S22.T22.C88.IMG1}}
$1$. Vidisha has $24$ tickets in $6\text{ units}$, and $24 \div 6$ gives $4$ tickets per unit; check Jabalpur: $5 \times 4 = 20$
$2$. Sagar $16 \div 4$ gives $4\text{ units}$
$3$. Seoni $16 \div 4$ gives $4\text{ units}$, so its bar is correct
$4$. Indore $28 \div 4$ gives $7\text{ units}$, so its bar is too short and must be redrawn
Answer: $(a)$: $24$; $(b)$: $20$; $(c)$: $1\text{ unit}$ length $= 4$ tickets; $(d)$: Sagar bar $4\text{ units}$ tall $(16)$; $(e)$: Axis $0$, $4$, $8$, $12$, $16$, $20$, $24$, $28$; $(f)$: Seoni correct, Indore incorrect (should be $7\text{ units}$ for $28$)

topics.summary: A table keeps every number, a pictograph shows the data at a glance, and a bar graph compares frequencies fast; the scale is chosen from the smallest and the largest value.

content.text:
Like pictographs, bar graphs give a nice visual way to represent data. They represent data through equally-spaced bars, each of equal width, where the lengths or heights give frequencies of the different categories.
Each category is represented by a bar where the length or height depicts the corresponding frequency (for example, cost) or quantity (for example, runs).
The bars have uniform spaces between them to indicate that they are free standing and represent equal categories.
The bars help in interpreting data much faster than a frequency table. By reading a bar graph, we can compare frequencies of different categories at a glance.
We must decide the scale (for example, 1 unit length = 1 student or 1 unit length = ₹ 200) for a bar graph on the basis of the data including the minimum and maximum frequencies, so that the resulting bar graph fits nicely and looks visually appealing on the paper or poster we are preparing. The markings of the unit lengths as per the scale must start from zero.

content.text:
$1$. Class $8$ has the least, $6$ girls

media.title: Honest Graph Checker
media.context: Class 6 NCERT Ganita Prakash ch 4 'Data Handling and Presentation' (Choosing and Presenting Well). Measure each picture. Is it honest? Viral_V3 tool, ported from its standalone HTML.
media.description: Honest Graph Checker. Measure each picture. Is it honest? Authored rounds, no modes and no question bank: the child acts on the board, then answers; a header with points, hint, sound and home; a task card with Check; a message pill; step dots; Next / Finish; a finish screen with stars. Everything starts raw and changes only when the child acts. English, Hindi and Gujarati.

tool_config.idea: A decorated graph is honest only if its pictures show the same numbers as the table, so every picture is checked against the table.
tool_config.title: Honest Graph Checker
tool_config.screen: The mountain table beside a plain column graph and a triangle picture; a ruler line that measures heights and widths; a doubling check; a vertical or horizontal bar chooser.
feedback: A picture judged honest without a check shows the ruler first and asks for a measurement.
A misleading picture is shown next to the equal-width bars for the same table.
A solved card shows the table value, the picture value and the check.
challenges: Plain column graph: which mountain is tallest (Everest).
Triangle picture: do taller triangles also get wider (yes, so it misleads about width).
Is Everest twice as tall as Elbrus? Double 5642 (11284, more than 8848, so no).
Heights of the tallest persons in each class: vertical or horizontal bars (vertical).
Lengths of the longest rivers: vertical or horizontal bars (horizontal).
Denali 6194 m and Kilimanjaro 5895 m: how much taller is Denali (299 m).

content.text:
In addition to the steps described in previous sections, there are also some other more artistic and aesthetic aspects one can consider when preparing visual presentations of data to make them more interesting and effective. First, when making a visual presentation of data such as a pictograph or bar graph, it is important to make it fit in the intended space; this can be controlled, for example, by choosing the scale appropriately, as we have seen earlier. It is also desirable to make the data presentation visually appealing and easy-to-understand, so that the intended audience appreciates the information being conveyed.
Let us consider an example. Here is a table naming the tallest mountain on each continent, along with the height of each mountain in meters.
How much taller is Mount Everest than Mount Koscuiszko? Are Mount Denali and Mount Kilimanjaro very different in height? This is not so easy to quickly discern from a large table of numbers.
As we have seen earlier, we can convert the table of numbers into a bar graph, as shown on the right. Here, each value is drawn as a horizontal box. These are longer or shorter depending on the number they represent. This makes it easier to compare the heights of all these mountains at a glance.
However, since the boxes represent heights, it is better and more visually appealing to rotate the picture, so that the boxes grow upward, vertically from the ground like mountains. A bar graph with vertical bars is also called a column graph. Columns are the pillars you find in a building that hold up the roof.
Below is a column graph for our table of tallest mountains. From this column graph, it becomes easier to compare and visualise the heights of the mountains.
In general, it is more intuitive, suggestive and visually appealing to represent heights, that are measured upwards from the ground, using bar graphs that have vertical bars or columns. Similarly, lengths that are parallel to the ground (for example, distances between location on Earth) are usually best represented using bar graphs with horizontal arcs.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Mount Everest is 8848 m and Mount Koscuiszko is 2228 m. How much taller is Everest, and can you see it quickly in a table?
2. From the numbers, 8848 − 2228 = 6620 m, but in a long table this takes effort.
3. Draw the table as a bar graph and the difference is seen at a glance. Heights go up from the ground, so vertical bars, called a column graph, suit them.
4. Lengths along the ground, such as the length of a river, are best shown with horizontal bars.

concepts.concept_name: From a table of numbers to a column graph

content.text:
When data visualisations such as bar graphs are further beautified with more extensive artistic and visual imagery, they are called information graphics or infographics for short. The aim of infographics is to make use of attention-attracting and engaging visuals to communicate information even more clearly and quickly, in a visually pleasing way.
As an example of how infographics can be used to communicate data even more suggestively, let us go back to the table above listing the tallest mountain on each continent. We drew a bar graph with vertical bars (columns) rather than horizontal bars, to be more indicative of mountains. But instead of rectangles, we could use triangles, which look a bit more like mountains. And, we can add a splash of colour as well. Here is the result.
While this infographic might look more appealing and suggestive at first glance, it does have some issues. The goal of our bar graph earlier was to represent the heights of various mountains, using bars of the appropriate heights but the same widths. The purpose of using the same widths was to make it clear that we are only comparing heights. However, in this infographic, the taller triangles are also wider! Are taller mountains always wider? The infographic is implying additional information that may be misleading and may or may not be correct. Sometimes going for more appealing pictures can also accidentally mislead.
Taking this idea further, and to make the picture even more visually stimulating and suggestive, we can further change the shapes of the mountains to make them look even more like mountains, and add other details, while attempting to preserve the heights. For example, we can create an imaginary mountain range that contains all these mountains.
Is the infographic below better than the column graph with rectangular columns of equal width? The mountains look more realistic, but is the picture accurate?

diagram_spec.alt_text: A flat drawing of a mountain range with seven labelled peaks, Everest on the left looking about twice as tall as Elbrus, and the small Koscuiszko peak in front at the right.
diagram_spec.render_note: The page picture (p.32) is a shaded illustration with no axis, no scale and no ground line, so apparent heights cannot be read from it exactly. Measured on the page picture, summit heights above the bottom edge of the picture give Everest / Elbrus about 1.6, but above a ground line at the foot of the peaks they give 2.0, which is what the book and the LP say the picture shows ('Everest appears to be twice as tall as Elbrus'). The spec therefore draws Everest's summit exactly twice as high as Elbrus's above one ground line (10.0 and 5.0 drawing units; the true ratio 8848 / 5642 is about 1.57). The other summits keep the page order and the rough relative heights read from the page against that ground line (Aconcagua 7.1, Denali 5.9, Kilimanjaro 5.4, Vinson Massif 3.7); Koscuiszko is drawn as a small separate front peak (2.0, the lowest, as on the page). These drawing heights are not data; the figure has no scale. The ridge outline is a flat simplification of the page's shaded range. Book discrepancies: the page prints Kilimanjaro as 5892m, while the table (p.28), the graphs (p.29), the triangle infographic (p.31) and the LP print 5895m: this spec uses 5895m. The page spells Kosciuszko, while the LP and p.28-31 spell Koscuiszko: this spec follows the LP.
diagram_spec.reason: The question asks about 'the infographic below' (the illustrated mountain range, in which Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus); the plan shows that picture nowhere and the question cannot be judged without seeing it. The second block of this card (5642 x 2) is arithmetic and needs no picture; the single card diagram goes with the first block.

topics.summary: Data, tally marks and frequencies, pictographs with a key, bar graphs with a scale, and care with pictures that decorate a graph.

content.text:
Facts, numbers, measures, observations and other descriptions of things that convey information about those things is called data.
Data can be organised in a tabular form using tally marks for easy analysis and interpretation.
Frequencies are the counts of the occurrences of values, measures or observations.
Pictographs represent data in the form of pictures, or objects or parts of objects. Each picture represents a frequency which can be 1 or more than 1, this is called the scale and it must be specified.
Bar graphs have bars of uniform width; the length or height that indicates the total frequency of occurrence. The scale that is used to convert length or height to frequency again, must be specified.
Choosing the appropriate scale for a pictograph or bar graph is important to accurately and effectively convey the desired information or data and to also make it visually appealing.
Other aspects of a graph also contribute to its effectiveness and visual appeal such as how colours are used, what accompanying pictures are drawn, and whether the bars are horizontal or vertical. These aspects correspond to the artistic and aesthetic side of data handling and presentation.
However, making visual representations of data 'fancy' can also sometimes be misleading.
By reading pictographs and bar graphs accurately, we can quickly understand and make inferences about the data presented.

objectives.objective_text: Students say that the way to find the most popular game is to ask each classmate the same question and write the answers in a list, and name that list as data.
Students group a long list of favourite games by game, count each group, and name the game with the highest count as the most popular.
Students decide which questions need data collection, find the most popular choice from a list by counting, and plan a survey of their own class.
Students count each answer with a tally stroke, cross four strokes with a fifth to make a bundle of five, and read the total of a row of tally marks.
Students call the total of a tally row its frequency, use a frequency table to read how many chose each sweet, and say what the table cannot tell, such as which child chose which sweet.
Students tally a stream of answers on the tool into bundles of five, read each total as a frequency, and name the most and least chosen item.
Students arrange the shoe sizes of a class in ascending order and read off the smallest size, the largest size and how many students wear each size.
Students turn an ordered list into a frequency table by counting each value, and compare what each arrangement shows more easily.
Students order shoe sizes, answer questions from the ordered list, say why ordering helps, and tabulate trees and letters from their own surroundings.
Students read a pictograph where one smiley is one student, and name the mode of travel used by the most and by the fewest students.
Students read the key of a pictograph, multiply the symbols by it, and count a half symbol as half of the key.
Students read the key on the tool, turn symbols and half symbols into numbers, and answer questions about the most, the least and the total.
Students see why one symbol for each student needs too many symbols for large numbers, and choose a key such as one smiley for 5 students that saves time and space.
Students use a half smiley for 5 students when the key is 10, and explain why 33 or 27 students cannot be shown exactly.
Students choose a key on the tool, place the symbols and half symbols for each category, and check the pictograph against the table.
Students read the height of each bar against the equally spaced lines, find how many students were absent in a class, and name the class with the most and the class with none absent.
Students read a horizontal bar graph where one unit of length is 100 vehicles, find the busiest and the quietest hour, and add two bars read from the graph.
Students read a bar graph in crores with one unit of length for 10 crores, and find the increase over fifty years and in each decade by subtracting readings.
Students read the scale on the tool, read bar lengths as numbers, and answer questions about the most, the least, totals and differences.
Students draw the two lines, write the categories with equal spacing, choose the scale 1 unit for 1 student, and draw each bar as high as its frequency.
Students choose the scale 1 unit length = 10 runs for scores from 0 to 100, and divide each score by 10 to get the bar heights.
Students draw a bar graph of a family budget with 1 unit length = ₹ 200, and use it to find the most and second most spent items and to compare amounts.
Students pick a scale on the tool, drag each bar to its height, label the axes, and read totals and comparisons off the graph they made.
Students say what each of a table, a pictograph and a bar graph shows best, and choose the scale from the smallest and the largest frequency, starting from zero.
Students build frequency tables with tally marks, read and draw pictographs, and use totals, differences and halves to answer questions about the data.
Students see that a table of mountain heights makes it hard to compare quickly, draw it as bars, and choose vertical bars for heights measured upward.
Students say that an infographic adds pictures to a bar graph, and explain that triangles that grow wider with height tell something the data does not.
Students check the claim that Everest looks twice as tall as Elbrus by doubling 5642 and comparing with 8848.
Students compare a bar graph with its decorated version on the tool, check each picture against the table, and choose vertical or horizontal bars for given data.
Students restate what data and frequency mean, how tally marks organise data, how a key and a scale turn symbols and bars into numbers, and why pictures can mislead.

Book item: What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates?
Book item: What is the most popular game in their class?
Book item: Try to find out the most popular game among your classmates.

Book item: Pari wants to respond to the questions given below. Put a tick for the questions where she needs to carry out data collection and a cross for the questions where she doesn't need to collect data. Discuss your answers in the classroom. a. What is the most popular TV show among her classmates? b. When did India get independence? c. How much water is getting wasted in her locality? d. What is the capital of India? a) What is the most popular TV show among her classmates? b) When did India get independence? c) How much water is getting wasted in her locality? d) What is the capital of India?

Book item: Complete the table to help Shri Nilesh to purchase the correct numbers of sweets. a. How many students chose jalebi? b. Barfi was chosen by __ students? c. How many students chose gujiya? d. Rasgulla was chosen by __ students? e. How many students chose gulab jamun? Table: Table: Sweets / Tally marks / No. of students. Jalebi: 5-bar tally + 1 stroke = 6. Gulab jamun: 5-bar tally + 4 strokes = 9. Gujiya: two 5-bar tallies + 3 strokes (blank in book; =13). Barfi: 3 strokes (blank; =3). Rasgulla: 5-bar tally + 2 strokes (blank; =7). a) How many students chose jalebi? b) Barfi was chosen by __ students? c) How many students chose gujiya? d) Rasgulla was chosen by __ students? e) How many students chose gulab jamun?
Book item: Is the above table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student? Explain. If it is not sufficient, what is the alternative?

Book item: Sushri Sandhya noted shoe sizes of her students: Shoe-size grid (3 rows x 9): row1 4 5 3 4 3 4 5 5 4; row2 5 5 4 5 6 4 3 5 6; row3 4 6 4 5 7 5 6 4 5 (27 students). She arranged them in ascending order: 3, 3, 3, 4 (nine 4s), 5 (ten 5s), 6, 6, 6, 6, 7. Help her figure out: a. The largest shoe size in the class is __. b. The smallest shoe size in the class is __. c. There are __ students who wear shoe size 5. d. There are __ students who wear shoe sizes larger than 4. a) The largest shoe size b) The smallest shoe size c) Students who wear size 5 d) Students who wear sizes larger than 4
Book item: How did arranging the data in ascending order help to answer these questions?
Book item: Are there other ways to arrange the data?

Book item: Write the names of a few trees you see around you. When you observe a tree on the way from your home to school (or while walking from one place to another), record the data and fill in the following table (Tree / No. of Trees; rows Peepal, Neem, ..., ...). a. Which tree was found in the greatest number? b. Which tree was found in the smallest number? c. Were there any two trees found in the same numbers? a) Which tree was found in the greatest number? b) Which tree was found in the smallest number? c) Were there any two trees found in the same numbers?

Book item: Take a blank piece of paper and paste any small news item from a newspaper. Each student may use a different article. Now, prepare a table on the piece of paper as given below. Count the number of each of the letters 'c', 'e', 'i', 'r', and 'x' in the words of the news article, and fill in the table. Table: Letter | c | e | i | r | x | Any other letter of your choice; row 'Number of times found in the news item' (empty). a. The letter found the most number of times is __. b. The letter found the least number of times is __. c. List the five letters 'c','e','i','r','x' in ascending order of frequency. Now compare the order of your list with that of your classmates. Is your order the same or nearly the same as theirs? (Almost everyone is likely to get the order 'x, c, r, i, e'.) Why do you think this is the case? d. Write the process you followed to complete this task. e. Discuss with your friends the processes they followed. f. If you do this task with another news item, what process would you follow? a) The letter found the most number of times is __ b) The letter found the least number of times is __ c) List the five letters in ascending order of frequency; compare with classmates; why? d) Write the process you followed e) Discuss with friends the processes they followed f) If you do this task with another news item, what process would you follow?
Book item: Based on the picture, answer: Which mode of travel is used by the most number of students?
Book item: Which mode of travel is used by the least number of students?

Book item: Nand Kishor collected responses from the children of his middle school in Berasia regarding how often they slept at least 9 hours during the night. He prepared a pictograph (key: triangle = 10 children): Always 5 triangles; Sometimes 2 triangles and a half triangle; Never 4 triangles. Answer using the pictograph: 1. What is the number of children who always slept at least 9 hours at night? 2. How many children sometimes slept at least 9 hours at night? 3. How many children always slept less than 9 hours each night? Explain how you got your answer. 1) Children who always slept at least 9 hours 2) Children who sometimes slept at least 9 hours 3) Children who always slept less than 9 hours (Never)

Book item: The following pictograph shows the number of books borrowed by students, in a week, from the library of Middle School, Ginnori (Pictograph, key: open-book symbol = 1 book. Monday 5, Tuesday 4, Wednesday 2, Thursday 0 (empty row), Friday 5, Saturday 8.) a. On which day were the minimum number of books borrowed? b. What was the total number of books borrowed during the week? c. On which day were the maximum number of books borrowed? What may be the possible reason? a) Day with minimum books borrowed b) Total books borrowed in the week c) Day with maximum books; possible reason

Book item: Jarina and Sangita have the table of students present (Class I 30, II 35, III 20, IV 25, V 30, VI 25, VII 30, VIII 20). If they want to show their data through a pictograph, where they also use one symbol (smiley) for each student, as Lakhanpal did, what are the challenges they might face?
Book item: What could be the problems faced in preparing such a pictograph, if the total number of students present in a class is 33 or 27?

Book item: Magan Bhai sells kites at Jamnagar. Six shopkeepers from nearby villages come to purchase kites from him. The number of kites he sold to these six shopkeepers are given below: Table: Chaman 250, Rani 300, Rukhsana 100, Jasmeet 450, Jetha Lal 250, Poonam Ben 700 kites. Prepare a pictograph using the symbol (kite) to represent 100 kites. Answer: a. How many symbols represent the kites that Rani purchased? b. Who purchased the maximum number of kites? c. Who purchased more kites, Jasmeet or Chaman? d. Rukhsana says Poonam Ben purchased more than double the number of kites that Rani purchased. Is she correct? Why? a) Symbols for Rani b) Maximum kites c) Jasmeet or Chaman d) Is Rukhsana correct?

Book item: Answer the following questions using the bar graph: In Class 2, __ students were absent that day. (Bar graph 'No. of students absent in each class', 1 unit length = 1 student. Class 1:3, 2:5, 3:4, 4:2, 5:0, 6:1, 7:5, 8:7. y-axis Number of students 0-8; x-axis Class.)
Book item: In which class were the maximum number of students absent? __
Book item: Which class had full attendance that day? __

Book item: A bar graph shows the population of India in each decade over 50 years, in crores: 1951: 36, 1961: 44, 1971: 54, 1981: 68, 1991: 84, 2001: 102. The scale is 1 unit length for 10 crores, so a bar of 5 units shows 50 crores and a bar of 8 units shows 80 crores. How much did the population of India increase over 50 years? How much did it increase in each decade?

Book item: How many total cars passed through the crossing between 6 a.m. and noon? (Bar graph: Horizontal bar graph, one unit of length = 100 vehicles; y-axis Time intervals, x-axis Number of vehicles (100 to 1200). 6-7: about 150; 7-8: 1200; 8-9: 1000; 9-10: about 800; 10-11: about 700; 11-12: about 600.)
Book item: Why do you think so little traffic occurred during the hour of 6-7 a.m., as compared to the other hours from 7 a.m.-noon?
Book item: Why do you think the traffic was the heaviest between 7-8 a.m.?
Book item: Why do you think the traffic was lesser and lesser each hour after 8 a.m. all the way until noon?

Book item: The number of runs scored by Smriti in each of the 8 matches: Match 1 80, Match 2 50, Match 3 10, Match 4 100, Match 5 90, Match 6 0, Match 7 90, Match 8 50. Draw a bar graph. Minimum score 0, maximum 100; choose scale.

Book item: Monthly expenditure of Imran's family: House rent 3000, Food 3400, Education 800, Electricity 400, Transport 600, Miscellaneous 1200 (in rupees). Represent as a bar graph using 1 unit length = ₹ 200.

Book item: Using Imran's family bar graph (House rent 3000, Food 3400, Education 800, Electricity 400, Transport 600, Miscellaneous 1200): On which item does Imran's family spend the most and the second most?
Book item: Is the cost of electricity about one-half the cost of education? (Electricity 400, Education 800.)
Book item: Is the cost of education less than one-fourth the cost of food? (Education 800, Food 3400.)

Book item: Samantha visited a tea garden and collected data of insects and critters: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2. Help her prepare a bar graph representing this data.

Book item: Pooja collected data on tickets sold at Bhopal railway station for a few cities of Madhya Pradesh in two hours: Vidisha 24, Jabalpur 20, Seoni 16, Indore 28, Sagar 16. Her bar graph has a portion erased: no scale numbers on the vertical axis, Sagar bar missing; Vidisha bar is 6 units, Jabalpur 5 units, Seoni about 4 units, Indore about 4.5 units. a) Write the number of tickets sold for Vidisha above the bar. b) Write the number of tickets sold for Jabalpur above the bar. c) The bar for Vidisha is 6 unit lengths and the bar for Jabalpur is 5 unit lengths. What is the scale for this graph? d) Draw the correct bar for Sagar. e) Add the scale of the bar graph by placing the correct numbers on the vertical axis. f) Are the bars for Seoni and Indore correct in this graph? If not, draw the correct bar(s).

Book item: A survey of 120 students on preferred free-time activity: Playing 45, Reading story books 30, Watching TV 20, Listening to music 10, Painting 15. Draw a bar graph taking 1 unit length = 5 students. Which activity is preferred by most students other than playing?

Book item: Saplings planted in the first week of July (bar graph): Monday 50, Tuesday 40, Wednesday 30, Thursday 40, Friday 50, Saturday 60, Sunday 40. a. The total number of saplings planted on Wednesday and Thursday is ___. b. The total number planted during the whole week is ___. c. The greatest number were planted on ___ and the least on ___. Why do you think that is the case? Why were more saplings planted on certain days and fewer on others? What are the possible explanations? How could you check them?

Book item: Tigers in India (approx.) 2006 1400, 2010 1700, 2014 2200, 2018 3000, 2022 3700. Shagufta and Divya made a frequency table and a bar graph, but the graph has a few mistakes. Find the mistakes and fix them.

Book item: Chinu listed the means of transport that passed in front of his house from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m. (50 entries, see figure). a. Prepare a frequency distribution table. b. Which means of transport was used the most? c. If you were there to collect this data, how could you do it? Write the steps or process. a) Prepare a frequency distribution table for the data. b) Which means of transport was used the most? c) If you were there to collect this data, how could you do it? Write the steps or process.

Book item: Roll a die 30 times and record the number you obtain each time. Prepare a frequency distribution table using tally marks. Find the number that appeared: a. The minimum number of times. b. The maximum number of times. c. Find numbers that appeared an equal number of times. a) The minimum number of times. b) The maximum number of times. c) Find numbers that appeared an equal number of times.

Book item: Faiz prepared a frequency distribution table of wickets taken by Jaspreet Bumrah in his last 30 matches: wickets 0:2 matches, 1:4, 2:6, 3:8, 4:3, 5:5, 6:1, 7:1. a) What information is this table giving? b) What may be the title of this table? c) What caught your attention in this table? d) In how many matches has Bumrah taken 4 wickets? e) Mayank says, if we want the total wickets we add 0, 1, 2, 3 ..., up to 7. Can Mayank get the total number of wickets this way? Why? f) How would you correctly figure out the total number of wickets using this table?

Book item: Pictograph of tractors in five villages (1 symbol = 1 tractor): Village A 6, Village B 5, Village C 8, Village D 3, Village E 6. a. Which village has the smallest number of tractors? b. Which has the most? c. How many more tractors does Village C have than Village B? d. Komal says Village D has half the number of tractors as Village E. Is she right? a) Which village has the smallest number of tractors? b) Which village has the most tractors? c) How many more tractors does Village C have than Village B? d) Komal says, Village D has half the number of tractors as Village E. Is she right?

Book item: Pictograph of girl students in classes 1 to 8 (1 symbol = 4 girls; half symbol = 2 girls): Class 1 six symbols = 24, Class 2 four and a half = 18, Class 3 five = 20, Class 4 three and a half = 14, Class 5 two and a half = 10, Class 6 four = 16, Class 7 three = 12, Class 8 one and a half = 6. a. Which class has the least number of girls? b. Difference between the number of girls in Classes 5 and 6? c. If two more girls were admitted in Class 2, how would the graph change? d. How many girls are in Class 7? a) Which class has the least number of girl students? b) What is the difference between the number of girls in Classes 5 and 6? c) If two more girls were admitted in Class 2, how would the graph change? d) How many girls are there in Class 7?

Book item: Mudhol dogs in six villages: A 18, B 36, C 12, D 48, E 18, F 24. Prepare a pictograph and answer: a. What will be a useful scale or key? b. How many symbols represent the dogs in Village B? c. Kamini said that the dogs in Village B and Village D together will be more than the dogs in the other 4 villages. Is she right? Give reasons. a) What will be a useful scale or key to draw this pictograph? b) How many symbols will you use to represent the dogs in Village B? c) Kamini said B and D together have more dogs than the other 4 villages. Is she right? Give reasons.
Book item: How much taller is Mount Everest than Mount Koscuiszko? (Everest 8848 m, Koscuiszko 2228 m.)
Book item: Are Mount Denali and Mount Kilimanjaro very different in height? (Denali 6194 m, Kilimanjaro 5895 m.) The book says this is not easy to see quickly from a table of numbers.
Book item: In the triangle infographic the taller triangles are also wider. Are taller mountains always wider?
Book item: Is the infographic below better than the column graph with rectangular columns of equal width? The mountains look more realistic, but is the picture accurate?
Book item: What is 5642 × 2? (Everest appears twice as tall as Elbrus; Elbrus is 5642 m, Everest 8848 m.)
Book item: If you wanted to visually represent the data of the heights of the tallest persons in each class in your school, would you use a graph with vertical bars or horizontal bars? Why?

Book item: If you were making a table of the longest rivers on each continent and their lengths, would you prefer a bar graph with vertical bars or horizontal bars? Why? Try finding out this information, and then make the corresponding table and bar graph! Which continents have the longest rivers?

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's order. A question about the class gives a list, counting turns the list into a table, and the table is then shown as a pictograph and as a bar graph, with the scale as the idea that ties the pictures to the numbers.

points.text: Every graph starts from a question such as which game is most popular, so the data is collected, counted and ordered before it is drawn.
points.title: Ask a question, then collect

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: worked videos for the book's examples, a tool only where handling the data is the idea, then the book's Figure it Out questions in a practice topic, each with its own video.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic

points.text: A symbol or a unit of bar length always stands for a number. Reading and drawing both start by finding that number.
points.title: The scale tells the story

points.text: The common wrong ideas, such as 'the longest list entry is the most popular' or 'a bar of 6 units is always 6', are raised by Keeko and fixed with a count or a scale, never just a rule.
points.title: Keeko's doubts

chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
